verdict: Avoid new FMCG-distribution exposure in Haridwar for now; the local demand signal is too weak to offset the sector's national momentum, so only lend to the strongest sub-wholesalers with tight structure, and decline the rest.
title: Haridwar FMCG distribution: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
A Haridwar FMCG distributor buys van-loads of branded staples, biscuits, soaps and beverages from company depots, warehouses them, and pushes them to kirana shops, chemists and roadside dhabas on fixed routes. **Cash turns on the route, not on the shelf: the distributor's real asset is the delivery van and the retailer relationship, not the godown.** Margin is a fixed trade discount off MRP plus company schemes; pricing power sits with the brand, not the borrower. Working capital is the whole game: stock sits 15-30 days, retailers pay in 7-15 days, and the company wants payment on depot lift. So when a proposal lands, check the scheme-credit cycle and the route-wise outstanding, not just the turnover figure.

## What has changed now
**The local demand signal is the problem, not the sector.** Uttarakhand GST collections are down 19.1% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1%, a 25.2 pp gap [D], and state electricity demand grew 4.7% versus India's 9.5% [D]. Both point to a state economy running well below the national line. Nationally the FMCG peers are fine — Q1FY27 revenue growth accelerated to around 15% Y-o-Y from 11% in Q4FY26 [5], and Q2 saw consumer demand gather momentum for Marico, Godrej Consumer and retailers [4] — but that is a peer result, not a Haridwar fact. **Do not let a good national FMCG print talk you into a weak local balance sheet.** The local sources say little about Haridwar distribution specifically: one trader-awareness piece on food-safety standards ahead of the festive season [1] and one company-promise dispute [2]; treat both as colour, not credit evidence.

Avoid the single-brand, single-godown operator whose entire turnover depends on one company's festive push, and avoid anyone whose growth is coming from credit extended to retailers rather than from route sales. If a proposal shows receivables stretching beyond the stated retailer terms, ask for the route-wise ageing before you sanction.

## How to grow safely
**Structure on the cash cycle: cash credit sized to 30 days of purchases, not to annual turnover, with a 25% margin.** Take monthly stock-and-receivables statements, monthly GST returns, and route-wise sales; take the van hypothecation and a personal guarantee. Because the repo is at 5.5% with a tightening stance [D], price for a rise rather than a cut. Nationally bank credit is growing 29.1% against activity of 6.1% [D], so the system is lending far ahead of the real economy — that is exactly the environment where a distributor's turnover can look healthy while its cash is stuck in retailer credit.

## Early-warning signs
- **GST returns falling below the invoiced turnover for two months** — pull the limit and ask for the purchase register. - **Retailer outstanding crossing the stated 7-15 day terms** — stop fresh depot lifts until the route is cleaned. - **Stock days rising while sales are flat** — scheme-loading, not demand; cut the drawing power. - **Any company-promise or scheme dispute with the brand** [2] — reassess the single-brand exposure immediately.

outstanding beyond stated terms -> freeze fresh depot lifts until route is cleaned
stock days rising with flat sales -> reduce limit, treat as scheme-loading
any dispute with the company [2] -> reassess single-brand exposure at once
Uttarakhand GST stays below India [D] -> hold new sanctions, renew only
